title: Cockenoe (de Long Island)
summary: Cockenoe was an interpreter, boundary expert, counselor, and whaler whose recorded work linked Long Island and Connecticut. His career includes defense of Shelter Island residents, paid land surveying, Montaukett diplomacy, and the coast’s working economy.
content:
Language, land, and a long working life

Cockenoe, also written Chekanow, Chekonnow, and Cockenoe-de-Long Island, was a Native interpreter and counselor whose named appearances run from the 1648 East Hampton purchase through the 1687 Montauk conveyance. His work connected Native communities with English towns around Long Island Sound. He translated, marked boundaries, represented residents threatened with removal, and worked in whaling.1

Neither his birth date nor his exact death date is established. William Wallace Tooker’s 1896 biography follows his career through 1687; it does not document a death in 1702 or 1703.1

John Eliot’s teacher: a life reconstructed from two records

John Eliot described a young Long Island man who had been captured during the Pequot War and was living in Richard Collicott’s household at Dorchester. The man taught Eliot words, interpreted for him, and helped translate prayers and scriptural passages. Eliot also taught him to read and write. His letter places Native linguistic knowledge at the foundation of this missionary work.1

Eliot did not name this teacher. Tooker identified him with Cockenoe by comparing the teacher’s origin, language skills, and departure with Cockenoe’s subsequent appearance as an interpreter. That influential identification remains a historical reconstruction. The named Long Island records provide the firmer outline of Cockenoe’s later career.1

1648–1652: East Hampton, Norwalk, and Shelter Island

The East Hampton purchase of April 29, 1648 explicitly appointed Chectanoo to interpret between the Native parties and English purchasers. The agreement retained Native hunting and fishing, shell gathering for wampum, and a share of stranded whales. Understanding those terms was central to the interpreter’s work.1 2

Tooker also traces Cockenoe in the Norwalk purchase recorded in February 1651/52. Across the Sound, his name survives in Cockenoe Island. The documentary association connects his career with Connecticut as well as Long Island.1 2

On September 2, 1652, Checkanoe addressed the United Colonies commissioners for the Native inhabitants of Shelter Island. They were being threatened with removal under a purchaser’s claimed title. He explained that they had given James Forrett only a portion marked by trees, without surrendering their homes. The commissioners referred the complaint to New Haven for examination.1 2

1657–1659: the expertise behind a boundary

Cockenoe witnessed the July 4, 1657 Hempstead confirmation involving Wyandanch and Tackapousha. Hempstead later appointed townsmen to accompany him in marking its bounds. Those proceedings connected his knowledge with the Merrick and Hempstead Plains landscape.4 3 5

The August 17, 1658 Huntington agreement specified separate compensation for his work marking three South Shore meadow necks: a coat, powder, lead, a hatchet, and wampum. Wyandanch’s receipt of May 23, 1659 refers back to the meadows Cockenoe had marked. He was a skilled participant with an explicit wage, not simply a name added to someone else’s deed.4 3 5

Testimony taken from Pauquatoun on October 18, 1667 recalled that Wyandanch had appointed Cockenoe and Sakkatakka to mark Rattaconeck land. Pauquatoun described seeing the marked trees and hearing Wyandanch approve the bounds. The testimony records Cockenoe’s work; it is not Cockenoe’s own deposition.4 3 5

1660–1670: Montaukett leadership after Wyandanch

Cockenoe appears with Wuchikittawbut, Wyancombone, Pauquatoun, and others in the August 1660 Montauk agreement. The widow’s January 1663 declaration again names him, this time with Tobis marking John Cooper’s beach limits so that payments for whales could be enforced.2 1

On November 3, 1669, Checkannoo and other Montaukett leaders rejected Ninigret’s claim that their people owed him submission and tribute. On December 1, 1670, Chekonnow joined the conveyance of land between Montauk’s ponds. These appearances show his continuing part in collective decisions after Wyandanch’s death.2 1

1675–1687: whaling, interpretation, and care of the landscape

A July 4, 1675 agreement placed Cockenoe in the whaling enterprise of James Schellinger and James Loper. The work included transporting the catch and trying out oil, with compensation expressed as a share of profits. His career therefore connects diplomatic and language work with the labor of the South Shore.1

In June 1677 he interpreted competing Native land claims before Governor Andros and the council. Montauk accounts in 1682 recorded payments for tending corn and burning the landscape. His mark appears again in the August 3, 1687 Montauk conveyance. These later records extend his story well beyond the episode with Eliot and show a working life sustained across several generations of colonial settlement.1

References

  1. Cockenoe-de-Long Island: documentary biography. William Wallace Tooker, John Eliot’s First Indian Teacher and Interpreter, Cockenoe-de-Long Island (1896): Eliot letters and the author’s identification; dated records of 1648, 1652, 1657–1659, 1667, 1669–1670, 1675, 1677, 1682, and 1687; notes 9–10, 20–25, 34–45, 70–82.
  2. East Hampton records: Wyandanch agreements and canoe case. Records of the Town of East-Hampton, vol. I (1887), pp. 2–3 (1648 purchase), 172–175 (August 1660 indenture and counterbond), 198 (December 1, 1662 statement), 199–200 (January 14, 1662/63 beach agreement).
  3. Huntington records: Wyandanch, Keeossechok and Cockenoe deeds. Huntington Town Records, vol. I (1887), pp. 10–13 (June 1 and July 23, 1657), 15–16 (May 14, 1658), 16–18 (August 17, 1658 and May 23, 1659).
  4. Hempstead confirmations signed by Wyandanch, 1657–1658. Records of the Towns of North and South Hempstead, Long Island, N.Y., vol. I (1896), pp. 45–48: July 4, 1657 confirmation, May 11, 1658 boundaries, and the son’s later confirmation.
  5. Smithtown records: Wyandanch family deed and land testimony. William S. Pelletreau, ed., Records of the Town of Smithtown (1898), pp. 1–2 (1650 Nasseconseke agreement), 3–5 (1659 family deed), 8–9 (1664 complaint and May 4, 1665 settlement), 16–17 (June 22, 1666 kinship testimony and October 18, 1667 boundary testimony).
why_this_matters: Cockenoe places Native language knowledge and diplomacy at the center of Long Island history. His work as an interpreter and boundary negotiator shaped records that colonial governments later used to claim land, making careful interpretation essential.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
